en: The Shorter Exposition:
The Exposition of the Chapter on the Way to the Far Shore;
The Exposition of the Questions.
16. The Exposition of the Questions of the Young Brahmin Piṅgiya “I am old,
weak, and my complexion has faded,” (said the Venerable Piṅgiya).
My vision is not clear and my hearing is not at ease;
lest I perish, bewildered along the way,
teach me the Dhamma so that I may understand it.
The complete abandoning of birth and aging in this world:
"I am old, weak, and my complexion has faded.
"I am old" means he is aged, advanced in years, elderly, come to the end of his journey, having reached the stage of life at one hundred and twenty years of age.
"Feeble" means weak, lacking strength, and lacking energy.
"Deprived of color" means deprived of complexion, devoid of complexion, and having lost one's complexion.
That former beautiful appearance has vanished, and the danger has become manifest.
"I am old, weak, and my complexion has faded"—thus spoke the Venerable Piṅgiya.
"Thus" (*icca*) is a grammatical conjunction (*padasandhi*)... [etc.]...
“Venerable” (*āyasmā*) is a term of endearment... [etc.
...“Piṅgiya” is the name of that brahmin... [etc. ...the utterance “thus”—this is why he is called “the venerable Piṅgiya.”
"The eyes are not pure, hearing is not comfortable" means that the eyes are impure, unclean, unpurified, and not bright.
"I do not see forms with the eye in such a way"—
thus, the eyes are not pure.
“Hearing is not comfortable” means the ear is impure, unpurified, not completely purified, and not bright.
“I do not hear sound with the ear in such a way”— thus,
the eyes are not pure and hearing is not comfortable.
"May I not perish, bewildered, in the interval. "May I not perish" means:
may I not perish, may I not be lost, may I not come to ruin, may I not disappear. "Bewildered" (momuho) means:
one whose face is turned toward delusion, one who has entered into ignorance, one who is ignorant, lacking discernment, and of poor wisdom.
“May I not perish, bewildered and midway, without having understood, attained, known, acquired, touched, and realized your Dhamma, your view, your practice, your path;
may I not pass away prematurely.
Explain the Dhamma so that I may know it.”
"Dhamma" refers to the holy life that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, entirely complete and pure; namely,
the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power,
the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the noble eightfold path, and Nibbāna.
"Explain, teach, describe, establish, reveal, analyze, clarify, and make manifest the path leading to Nibbāna"— thus,
"explain the Dhamma."
"‘Yamahaṃ vijaññaṃ’: may I know it, recognize it, discern it, understand it thoroughly, penetrate it, attain it, touch it, and realize it—teach me that Dhamma which I should know.
‘Jātijarāya idha vippahānaṃ’: the abandoning, the subsiding, the relinquishing, the stilling, the deathless Nibbāna, right here in this very life, of birth, aging, and death."
The complete relinquishing of birth and aging in this world.
Therefore, that brahmin said:
"I am old, weak, and my complexion has faded."
(Thus spoke the Venerable Piṅgiya:
"Guidance is not pure, nor is hearing at ease;
may I not perish, deluded, along the way."
"Explain the Dhamma so that I may understand it—
the relinquishing of birth and old age in this very world.
Having seen beings being afflicted amidst forms, [he spoke thus].
"O Piṅgiya, the Blessed One said:
People who are heedless are tormented by forms;
therefore, O Piṅgiya, you should be heedful."
"May he abandon form for the sake of non-rebirth.
Having seen that beings are afflicted by forms—
where "form" refers to the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements.
Beings are slain, tormented, afflicted, and struck down because of form, with form as the cause, and form as the condition.
When form exists, they inflict various punishments for their deeds:
they strike them with whips, they strike them with canes, they strike them with clubs, and they cut off their hands.
They cut off a foot; they cut off both hands and feet; they cut off an ear; they cut off a nose; they cut off both ears and nose;
they make them undergo the *bilaṅgathālika* torture; they make them undergo the *saṅkhamuṇḍika* torture;

they make them undergo the *rāhumukha* torture; they make them undergo the *jotimālika* torture; they make them undergo the *hatthapajjotika* torture; they make them undergo the *erakavattika* torture.
They make them wear garments of bark; they make them wear the skin of an antelope; they make them wear a fish-hook; they make them wear a coin;
they make them undergo the "salt-and-rasp" torture; they make them undergo the "rolling-pin" torture; they make them undergo the "bed of straw" torture;
they douse them with boiling oil; they have them devoured by dogs; and while still alive, they impale them on stakes.
They even cut off the head with a sword.
Thus, because of form, with form as condition, and with form as cause, beings are slain, struck down, afflicted, and harmed.

Having seen, having perceived, having weighed, having scrutinized, having analyzed, and having made manifest [this fact] while they are being slain, struck down, afflicted, and harmed—thus [he understands].
Having seen those who are distressed by forms,
[the Blessed One said: "O Piṅgiya," the Blessed One addressed that brahmin by name.
"Bhagavā" is a designation for one who possesses reverence... [and so on] ...it is a realization-based designation, namely "Bhagavā"—thus the Blessed One is called Piṅgiya.
"People who are heedless are afflicted by forms."
"They are afflicted" means they are afflicted, disturbed, oppressed, and struck; they become diseased and dejected.
They are afflicted, disturbed, oppressed, and struck by eye-disease; they become diseased and dejected. By ear-disease... [and so on].

They are broken, distressed, oppressed, and afflicted by bodily disease... and by contact with gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things; they become sick and dejected—thus they are "broken among forms" (ruppati rūpesu).
Alternatively, when the eye is wasting away, fading away, declining, becoming different, disappearing, and vanishing, they are afflicted... [and so on] ...they become sorrowful.
When the ear... [and so on] ...[is likewise].
In the nose … in the tongue … in the body …
In regard to forms … in regard to sounds … in regard to odors …
In taste … in tangible object … in family …
In the community...
in the residence... in gain...
In fame … in praise … in pleasure …
Regarding robes … regarding almsfood … regarding lodgings …

When the requisite of medicine as a support for the sick is diminishing, decreasing, wasting away, fading, disappearing, and vanishing, they suffer, are disturbed, are oppressed, are afflicted, and being diseased, they become dejected—
thus too they suffer in relation to forms (*rūpa*).
"People" (*jana*) refers to khattiyas, brahmins, vessas, suddas, householders, those gone forth, devas, and humans.
"Negligent" means negligence should be stated as either misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, or misconduct of mind;

or the relinquishing of the mind toward the five strands of sensual pleasure, the continued relinquishing [thereof], lack of earnestness in the cultivation of wholesome states, lack of constancy in practice,
lack of steadfastness in practice, a sluggish mode of conduct, and the casting aside of one's aspiration.
Laying down the burden, lack of cultivation, lack of development, lack of frequent practice, lack of resolve, lack of application, and negligence.
Whatever is such negligence, the act of being negligent, the state of being negligent—
this is called negligence (*pamāda*).
"Because people possessed of this negligence are called 'negligent,' negligent people are afflicted by forms.
Therefore, Piṅgiya, you too must be diligent."
Therefore, for that reason, by that cause, by that condition, by that source, seeing such danger in material forms—therefore, Piṅgiya, you should be heedful:
acting with diligence, acting with constancy... "Heedfulness regarding wholesome states"—thus it was said.
"Therefore, Piṅgiya, being heedful,
abandon form so as not to be born again.
"Form" refers to the four great elements and the form derived from the four great elements.
"Relinquish form": relinquish form, abandon form, dispel form, bring form to an end, cause form to cease to exist.

"For the sake of non-renewal of existence": so that this form of yours might cease right here, and no further existence with rebirth-linking might arise—whether in the sense-sphere realm, the fine-material realm, or the immaterial realm;
or in the existence of sense-desire, the existence of form, or the existence of the formless.

Whether in the realm of perception, the realm of non-perception, or the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; whether in a one-constituent existence, a four-constituent existence, or a five-constituent existence;

whether again in a destiny, a rebirth, a rebirth-linking, an existence, in saṃsāra, or in the round of becoming—he would not produce it, would not generate it, would not bring it about, would not cause it to arise, but would have it cease right here.
"May it be stilled, may it come to an end, may it subside"— thus,
"abandon form so that there is no further becoming.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Having seen those who are distressed amidst forms,
O Piṅgiya,” said the Blessed One,
“foolish people are afflicted by forms.”
"Therefore, Piṅgiya, being heedful,
abandon form so that there is no further becoming.
To the four cardinal directions and the four intermediate directions—
Above, below, and in these ten directions—
there is nothing in the world that is unseen, unheard, unperceived, or unknown by you.
"Declare the Dhamma so that I may understand it—the relinquishing here of birth and aging.
'The four quarters, the four intermediate directions, above and below—these are the ten directions. Thus, "the ten directions."

"There is nothing in the world that has not been seen, heard, sensed, or cognized by you"—this means that for you there is nothing whatsoever that has not been seen, heard, sensed, or cognized, whether it be one's own welfare, another's welfare, or the welfare of both;
whether it be a matter pertaining to this visible world or a matter pertaining to the future life; whether it be a shallow matter or a profound matter; or a matter that is hidden or concealed.
Whether it be a meaning that is yet to be inferred, a meaning that has been inferred, a meaning that is blameless, a meaning that is free from defilement, a meaning that is purified,

or a meaning that is the ultimate truth— if there were anything in the world that was not seen by you, not heard, not sensed, and not cognized, that would not exist, would not be present, would not be found, and would not be apprehended. But there is nothing such as that in the world.
"Proclaim the Dhamma so that I may know it. "Dhamma":

proclaim, teach, describe, establish, reveal, analyze, clarify, and explain the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, [good in the middle, and good in the end, with the meaning and the phrasing, and which reveals the perfectly complete and pure holy life], as well as Nibbāna and the practice leading to Nibbāna.
"‘May I know that which I should know’ means: may I know it, understand it, discern it, penetrate it, pierce through it, attain it, touch it, and realize it—teach me that Dhamma which I should know.
‘The complete abandoning of birth and aging here’ means: right here is the abandoning, the subsiding, the relinquishing, the calming, the deathless Nibbāna of birth, aging, and death."
The complete relinquishing of birth and aging in this world.
Therefore that brahmin said:
“The four cardinal directions and the four intermediate directions...”
Above, below, and in these ten directions—
there is nothing in the world that is unseen, unheard, unperceived, or unknown by you.
"Explain the Dhamma so that I may understand it—
the relinquishing here of birth and old age.
Observing human beings overcome by craving, [he said:]
(Thus spoke the Blessed One: "O Piṅgiya,
when one is born into suffering and overcome by old age,
therefore you, Piṅgiya, must be diligent."
"Abandon craving for the sake of non-rebirth.
Regarding the phrase "beholding human beings overcome by craving":
craving means craving for forms … [and so on] … craving for mental phenomena (*dhamma*).

"Overcome by craving" means overcome by craving, following after craving, pursued by craving, assailed by craving, fallen into craving, proceeding toward craving, mastered by it, and with mind consumed by it.
"Manuja" is a designation for sentient beings.
"Pekkhamāno" means looking, seeing, gazing, contemplating, and examining.
"Beholding human beings overcome by craving.
"Piṅgiya," said the Blessed One—
thus the Blessed One addressed that brahmin by name.
"Bhagavā" is a designation for one who possesses reverence... [and so on] ...it is a realization-based designation, namely "Bhagavā"—thus the Blessed One is called Piṅgiya.
"Born into suffering, overcome by old age."

"Born of anguish" means born of the anguish of birth, born of the anguish of aging, born of the anguish of illness, born of the anguish of death, born of the anguish of sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair; born of the anguish of the suffering of hell ... [and so on] ...
born of the anguish of the suffering of misfortune through wrong views; born of calamity, born of disaster, born of misfortune.
"Born of anguish":
overtaken by old age means touched by old age, overcome, bewildered, and possessed by it;
followed by birth, pursued by old age, overwhelmed by sickness, struck down by death—without protection, without shelter, without refuge, having become one who has no refuge.
"Born of torment and overcome by old age;
therefore, Piṅgiya, you too must be heedful.
"Therefore" means for that reason, for that cause, for that condition, for that source—seeing such danger thus, [one should be heedful] regarding craving.
Therefore, Piṅgiya,
you too should be heedful and act with thorough care...
"Heedfulness regarding wholesome states"— thus it was said.
"Therefore, Piṅgiya, being heedful,
abandon craving so that there is no further becoming.
"Craving" refers to craving for forms … [and so on] … craving for mental phenomena (*dhamma*).
"Abandon craving"—abandon craving, relinquish craving, dispel craving, bring craving to an end, cause craving to cease.
"For the sake of non-renewal of existence"—so that for you...
[as before] ...existence with renewed rebirth-linking may not arise in the sense-sphere realm, the fine-material realm, or the immaterial realm.
Whether in the realm of sense-desire, the realm of form, or the formless realm; whether in the realm of perception, the realm of non-perception, or the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
whether in a one-constituent existence, a four-constituent existence, or a five-constituent existence;
or again, in any destiny, rebirth, rebirth-linking, becoming, saṃsāra, or the cycle of existence—he would not produce, would not generate, and would not bring about [further existence].
"May it not be produced; may it cease right here, be stilled, go to its end, and be subsided"—thus, abandon craving so that there is no further becoming.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Beholding human beings overcome by craving,
(Piṅgiya, said the Blessed One,) born of anguish and enveloped by old age;”
"Therefore, Piṅgiya, being heedful,
abandon craving for the sake of no further becoming. At the conclusion of this verse,

for those many thousands of beings who shared the same aspiration, the same application, the same purpose, and were permeated by the same latent tendencies as the brahmin, the dustless, stainless Eye of Dhamma arose.
“Whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation.
And to that brahmin, the dustless, stainless eye of Dhamma arose:
“Whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation.”
Simultaneously with the acquisition of the Dhamma-eye, his antelope skin, matted hair, bark garments, triple staff, and water pot, as well as his head hair and beard,
disappeared; clothed in smooth saffron robes, wearing the outer cloak, bowl, and robes, he sat with palms joined in reverence,
honoring the Blessed One by practicing in accordance with the Dhamma.
“The Blessed One is my teacher, venerable sir; I am his disciple.
This is the sixteenth exposition: the Questions of the Young Brahmin Piṅgiya.
